title.es: Construir sobre la idea de otro

es: Aportar una opinión con acuerdo parcial, ampliar lo dicho por otro con un ejemplo y devolver el turno con una pregunta a otro participante.

origin.text: Mia: Screens distract children in class.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige cómo interviene Mia.

choices.text: She agrees in part, gives an example and asks Sara a question.
She agrees in part, gives an example and asks Tom a question.

feedback.es: Acepta parte de la idea, aporta un ejemplo y termina con una pregunta a Tom.

origin.audio: I agree with you in part, Tom. Tablets help, but they do not solve everything. For instance, my class was better organised, but nobody read more. Did you see a difference in your school?

prompt.es: Escribe tu intervención: acuerdo parcial, ampliación con ejemplo y una pregunta.

answer.text: Thank you, Tom. That is a valid point, and I agree with you up to a point. Phones do distract students, and nobody can deny it. But I see one drawback in a complete ban: many students use their phones to learn. For instance, last week my teacher asked us to record a short interview, and every group used a phone for it. Building on your idea, I would like to suggest a simple rule: phones stay in a box during explanations, and students can take them out when the teacher asks. Furthermore, we could ask the students to write the rules themselves. Seldom do people follow a rule that they did not help to make. Partly for that reason, I would not ban phones completely, but I would limit them clearly. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they need different rules? I would really like to hear your view before we decide anything.
accepted: Thank you, Tom. That is a valid point, and I agree with you up to a point. Phones do distract students, and nobody can deny it. But I see one drawback in a complete ban: many students use their phones to learn. For instance, last week my teacher asked us to record a short interview, and every group used a phone for it. Building on your idea, I would like to suggest a simple rule: phones stay in a box during explanations, and students can take them out when the teacher asks. Furthermore, we could ask the students to write the rules themselves. Seldom do people follow a rule that they did not help to make. Partly for that reason, I would not ban phones completely, but I would limit them clearly. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they need different rules? I would really like to hear your view before we decide anything.

Thanks, Tom. That is a fair point, and I partly agree with you, because phones really do distract us in class. However, I see a drawback: some lessons need a phone, for example to look up a word or take a photo of the board. For instance, yesterday we used a phone to record our science experiment. Building on your idea, I would suggest that phones stay in a bag, and that the teacher decides when we can use them. Furthermore, students should help to make the rules, because we follow what we choose. This is a valid way to limit the problem without a complete ban. Mia, what do you see with your younger students? Would the same rules work for them? I am curious about your experience, and I would like to hear it before we decide.

feedback.es: Una buena intervención reconoce lo válido, matiza el acuerdo, amplía con un ejemplo y devuelve el turno con una pregunta a Mia.

origin.text: Mesa redonda sobre el móvil en el aula. Tom dijo: «Los móviles deberían prohibirse en clase». Responde en inglés (unas 130–220 palabras): reconoce lo válido de su idea, expresa un acuerdo parcial (up to a point, partly), amplía con un ejemplo (for instance) y termina con una pregunta dirigida a otra participante, Mia.
